summary: Mydei gave up a guaranteed corporate empire to pursue racing, which means his life now consists of blistering speeds, unreasonable expectations, and pretending he’s completely normal about the figure skater he may or may not have admired for years. Phainon just came back from hiatus, has a dangerous lack of subtlety, and a habit of flirting without realizing he’s flirting—especially with the very attractive F1 driver who keeps making deeply specific comments about his past performances. “Your footwork in Shanghai was clean, too.” Phainon turns toward him fully this time, eyebrows lifting as he repeats the word. “Shanghai,” he says. “That was… a while ago.” Unfortunately for Mydei, the only person he won’t have to worry about teasing him is Phainon.

“Your footwork in Shanghai was clean, too.”

Phainon turns toward him fully this time, eyebrows lifting as he repeats the word.

“Shanghai,” he says. “That was… a while ago.”

Unfortunately for Mydei, the only person he won’t have to worry about teasing him is Phainon.

chapters.html:
Mydei almost dies at least six times before lunch.

This is not a complaint. This is simply how racing works.

At the Circuit de Barcelona-Catalunya, the sun hangs low and smug, baking the asphalt until it radiates heat like it’s holding a grudge. The track shimmers. The grandstands ripple. Somewhere in the distance, a flag waves with the enthusiasm of a tired fan who has been here since dawn and refuses to leave without compensation.

Inside Car 27, Mydei is cooking alive.

Spain has decided that race day is an appropriate time to turn the weather into a personal attack. His fireproof suit traps heat with surgical efficiency, sweat pooling along his spine, his gloves damp enough to be annoying but not dangerous. The visor fogs every time he exhales, as if the car itself is offended by human respiration.

At 312 kilometers per hour, this is still the least of his problems.

The world narrows.

Not into silence, because cars never shut up, but into something precise. The engine’s vibration hums through his bones. The steering wheel chatters in his hands. The tires scream their opinions at every corner entry, dramatic and unhelpful as always. Every sensation stacks on top of the other until thought becomes instinct and instinct becomes command.

Mydei thrives here.

“Front left degradation increasing,” Hephaestion says in his ear, voice steady in the way of a man who has already accepted that stress is a lifestyle choice. “Sixty-eight percent. ERS thirty-eight. Delta plus four-tenths to Morales.”

Santiago Morales.

Spain’s darling menace. Local hero. Late-braking menace with a smile so charming it should be illegal. The crowd adores him with the kind of loyalty usually reserved for football clubs and childhood pets.

They are being very loud about it.

Mydei flicks the wheel slightly, adjusting brake bias with the casual confidence of someone rearranging furniture he owns.

“I can take him.”

A pause.

Hephaestion exhales like a man counting to ten in multiple languages. “Box this lap unless you’re going for it at Turn Ten.”

“That sounds like permission.”

“It absolutely is not.”

“And yet.”

“And Perdikkas will personally superglue you to the simulator if you injure your shoulder again.”

Mydei considers this, accelerating through Turn Seven with elegant aggression. “He said that last time too.”

“That was also a direct quote. I edited out profanity.”

“…I appreciate your restraint.”

The garage exists somewhere far away, vibrating with stress and caffeine. Leonnius is pacing, no doubt. Ptolemy is probably writing numbers that mean something only to him. Perdikkas is preparing to commit an act of violence against the concept of recklessness.

They cannot talk to Mydei.

Race rules.

This is the quiet part.

This is his favorite part.

He charges toward Campsa, Turn Nine, a corner infamous for asking drivers deeply personal questions about their life choices, to which Mydei answers by taking it flat.

The car howls. The tires protest. G-force pins him back like an accusation.

He exhales, controlled, practiced. The visor fogs for half a second.

Annoying.

“DRS on exit. ERS deploy ready,” Hephaestion says, focused.

“I know.”

“You always know. I still have to say it.”

“Occupational hazard.”

“Please sound less arrogant while driving.”

“No promises.”

Ahead, Morales defends the racing line like it’s family property. His rear tires twitch under braking, old rubber begging for mercy. Mydei clocks it instantly, brain doing math faster than conscious thought.

Turn Ten approaches.

Heavy braking. Narrow entry. Glory or embarrassment.

Morales brakes early.

Mydei does not.

He opens DRS and the car lunges forward like it’s been insulted, speed surging, wind clawing at him. He feints outside, watches Morales commit, and then slices inside with surgical cruelty.

Late braking. Trail braking. The front tires flirt with disaster.

Mydei corrects with a tiny movement, elegant and instinctive, the kind of motion that looks effortless because it has been practiced to death.

The crowd erupts.

Morales gives him space. Barely. Enough.

Mydei slips through, slotting ahead like he belongs there.

Because he does.

He feels it then, sharp and bright in his chest, a flash of something dangerously close to joy.

Beautiful.

Hephaestion explodes in his ear. “YES—YES—THAT’S IT! THAT’S HOW YOU SEND A MAN INTO RETIREMENT WITHOUT TOUCHING HIM!”

Something crashes in the garage. A clipboard dies. Ptolemy mourns.

The rest of the race blurs into discipline and control. Tire management. Clean exits. Ignoring half of Hephaestion’s increasingly frantic reminders. Accepting a track limits warning with a hum and a promise to behave that means nothing.

When the checkered flag waves, Mydei crosses the line with a gap wide enough to feel intentional.

P1.

Everyone roars.

His heart stays steady.

“All clear,” Hephaestion says, voice wrecked with relief.

“Copy,” Mydei replies.

Inside the helmet, he smiles.

Somewhere in Barcelona, a barista is about to experience the single greatest iced coffee order of their career.

The first coherent thought Mydei has after crossing the finish line—after the crowd detonates into noise, after the fireworks bloom, after Hephaestion screams something over the radio that might technically qualify as a religious experience—is not noble.

It is not reflective, nor particularly patriotic.

It is not, in any way, befitting a race winner.

If they spray champagne directly into my eyes again, I will simply leave this plane of existence.

He lets the car roll into the cooldown lap, easing his grip on the wheel as adrenaline drains out of him in a warm, buzzing haze. His pulse still beats against the carbon fiber grips, steady and stubborn, like it refuses to accept that the danger part is over. Heat clings to him aggressively. Barcelona has been hot all weekend, but now it feels personal, like the city itself is trying to finish him off where the track failed.

Inside the suit, sweat has given up on subtlety. The fabric sticks. His gloves are soaked. His fireproof balaclava has reached a state best described as emotionally damp.

He exhales, slow and controlled, fogging the visor for half a second.

Annoying. Seriously annoying.

“You realize,” Hephaestion says in his ear, voice hoarse and vibrating with adrenaline he absolutely did not burn off himself, “that you just ruined at least three Spanish childhoods.”

“I thought I was being nice,” Mydei replies. “I left him room.”

“Uh-huh, sure.”

The radio crackles with overlapping voices now. Someone cheers. Someone else laughs a little hysterically. Ptolemy, unmistakable even through static, announces that he knew Turn Ten was the move and that he has the data to prove it, which no one asked for.

Hephaestion tries—and fails—to reassert radio discipline. “Alright, alright, deep breaths, everyone. Mydei, all clear. Bring it home.”

“I am literally already done.”

“Yes, and yet I still don’t trust you.”

Mydei hums in acknowledgment as he guides the car toward the pit lane. The crowd noise swells again, pressing in through the helmet, through the cockpit, through the bones in his skull. Flags wave. His name ripples across the grandstands, distorted and echoing, a thousand strangers shouting in unison.

He does not wave back.

That part comes later.

Parc fermé hits him like a wall of movement. Engineers swarm the car the moment it stops, practiced and precise, hands already on the chassis before the tires have finished whining. One mechanic taps the halo twice—quick, affectionate, ritualistic—and another gives him a thumbs-up that somehow manages to look deeply relieved.

Cameras descend immediately. Lenses everywhere. Red lights blinking like insects.

A marshal gestures for engine off.

Mydei kills the car, silence rushing in so suddenly it feels unreal. He removes the steering wheel with careful hands, ignoring the faint tremor in his fingers. Leftover electricity. It happens every time. He almost drops it anyway.

“Please don’t break anything important,” Leonnius calls from somewhere to his left, appearing out of the chaos as if he’s been stress-sprinting for the last two hours. “We’re already over budget on replacement parts.”

“I caught it,” Mydei mutters. “Have some faith.”

Leonnius snorts. “I had faith once. It didn’t survive Turn Seven.”

Mydei climbs out of the cockpit, boots hitting concrete, and the sound slams into him all at once. The crowd roars louder now that he’s visible, a physical thing that presses against his chest. Someone near the fence is waving a massive cutout of his face that looks like it was printed from a screenshot taken during turbulence.

He removes his gloves, folding them neatly despite the shake in his hands. He’s learned how to do that without thinking. He’s learned what cameras notice.

Perdikkas materializes at his side like an omen.

He drapes something over Mydei’s shoulders that technically qualifies as a flannel but is, in practice, the size of a ceremonial banner.

“Drink,” Perdikkas says, already shoving a bottle into his hands. “You underhydrated on lap forty-three.”

“I was busy,” Mydei replies, taking a sip anyway.

“You were reckless.”

“I was efficient.”

“You were one corner away from me committing a crime.”

Perdikkas leans in slightly, voice dropping. “If you do that again without telling me first, I will replace your steering wheel with a conscience.”

Mydei swallows another mouthful. “Noted.”

Peucesta slips in on his other side without announcing himself, like a shadow. He smells faintly of expensive lotion and impending press releases. A tablet rests in his hands, its screen a mosaic of timing sheets, sponsor notifications, and photos Mydei would prefer never see daylight.

“Smile,” Peucesta murmurs, adjusting the drape of the flannel with two precise fingers. “Just once.”

“I am smiling on the inside.”

“That does not monetize.”

Mydei sighs.

Peucesta tilts his head, eyes flicking briefly toward one of the cameras, then back to Mydei. “Your father is watching.”

That does it.

Mydei lifts the corners of his mouth into something small, controlled, and perfectly acceptable. It is not joy. It is not triumph. It is the kind of smile that says yes, I am alive, yes, I did the thing, please do not ask more of me.

The cameras eat it up.

Peucesta nods once, satisfied.

“Good,” he says. “We’ll go viral.”

Somewhere behind them, Hephaestion finally breaks free of the garage and barrels toward him, headset crooked, eyes bright. “That pass,” he says breathlessly, hands flying, “that was—my god, that was art.”

Mydei inclines his head. “I aim to please.”

“Don’t,” Perdikkas says flatly. “It encourages him.”

Mydei’s gaze drifts back toward the track. His heart has finally settled. The noise fades into something distant and manageable.

He stands there, wrapped in fabric and voices and expectation, grounded and steady in the aftermath.

Winner.

And somehow, already thinking about the next one.

The walk to the weigh-in station is less a walk and more a controlled evacuation.

The FIA corridor funnels him forward while reporters stack up behind the barrier like birds on a wire, voices flying over one another with absolutely no regard for acoustics or human survival.

“MYDEI—HOW DID YOU FIND THE MOVE ON MORALES?” ”IS THIS YOUR STRONGEST SEASON YET?” “ARE THE RUMORS ABOUT YOUR FAMILY TRUE?” “MYDEI—GREECE IS VERY PROUD—”

That last one is shouted with particular fervor, the accent unmistakable, and it cuts cleanly through the noise.

Mydei does not look over, but he does grimace internally.

He keeps his gaze forward, posture relaxed, stride unhurried, like this is not his personal gauntlet. He has learned, over time, that acknowledgment is blood in the water.

That does not stop the crowd.

Kids lean over the barriers, waving flags too big for their arms. One boy trips over his own sneakers trying to keep up, only to be hauled upright by a mortified parent. Someone has brought a megaphone and is using it exclusively to yell “MYDEI” at wildly inappropriate intervals.

A handmade sign bobs into view:

DRIVE FAST BUT SAFELY PLEASE MY MOM IS WORRIED

Mydei breaks.

Just a little.

He glances over and gives the kid a real smile, brief but unmistakable, lifting two fingers in acknowledgment. The boy loses his mind completely, jumping so hard his sign folds in half.

Peucesta clocks it from behind him and, mercifully, says nothing.

Inside the tent, the noise changes shape rather than volume.

Leonnius is mid-sentence, arms flailing.

“—I’m telling you, centimeters,” Leonnius says, hands slicing the air. “Centimeters from the apex cone. I saw my career flash before my eyes. Do you understand how stupid that was? How beautiful? How—”

“Almost isn’t clipping,” Mydei interrupts calmly, stepping onto the scale.

Perdikkas makes a noise of deep, personal offense. “Almost gives me paperwork. Clip it next time and at least make it worth the medical report.”

“You would enjoy that far too much,” Mydei replies.

“I enjoy job security,” Perdikkas snaps. “You threaten it weekly.”

Hephaestion slips in close once the officials are distracted, bumping Mydei’s arm with his own. It’s small, deliberate, grounding.

“Good job, Mydeimos,” he says, voice low and worn in the way of someone who has spent two hours clenching every muscle he owns. “Textbook disorder.”

Mydei hums. “You sound relieved.”

“I am. I aged five years.”

Everything collapses into motion after that.

The weigh-in. Helmet off. A mechanic nearly tackles him in a hug. Someone claps him on the back hard enough to make a point about posture. Ptolemy appears with red eyes and insists it’s pollen season despite being indoors. Peucesta replaces one water bottle with another like a magician with a hydration obsession.

By the time it’s over, Mydei feels wrung out but upright, which he considers a success.

The podium wait is mercifully uneventful.

No champagne ambush. His vision remains intact.

Morales nearly dislocates his shoulder in a congratulatory hug and laughs like he’s still halfway in the car. “You’re insane,” he says, delighted.

“You defended beautifully,” Mydei replies, sincere.

Then comes the interview pen.

The lights are brutal. The microphones multiply. Peucesta takes up position just behind his right shoulder, tablet in hand, expression neutral enough to be legally classified as a weapon.

The questions come in waves.

The British want tire degradation and sector deltas.

The Spanish want Morales—how hard he pushed, whether it surprised him, whether respect still stands.

The French start doing math out loud, already trying to crown a champion with three races left.

Then the cadence shifts.

The Greek journalists however, go straight for the jugular.

“Was your father present at today’s race?” “Would you care to comment on Castrum Kremnos’ most recent endorsement?” ”Do you see yourself returning to Greece following retirement—or sooner?” ”You’re young,” one of them adds, politely ruthless, “but there are conversations about succession. Is there any truth to that?”

The word succession lands with weight.

Mydei doesn’t flinch.

He answers the way he’s been trained to: clean lines, no excess. His focus is on the race. He’s grateful for the support. He’s proud of his heritage. He’s taking things one season at a time.

He gives them nothing they can quote out of context, nothing that can be underlined in red.

One voice presses closer anyway, earnest with intent.

“Is it true you’ve avoided your father’s last three calls?”

The mood sours noticeably.

Hephaestion steps forward smoothly, badge visible, tone crisp and final. “That’s enough. Driver to debrief.”

Peucesta is already there, guiding Mydei away with a hand at his elbow before anyone can pretend the question was harmless.

The noise dulls behind them.

Only then does Mydei let out a slow breath, controlled, like easing off the throttle at the end of a long straight.

“Welcome back to reality,” Peucesta says, scrolling through his tablet. “Podium, television studio, three sponsor photos. Then you’re briefly free.”

“Briefly?”

“Twenty minutes. Thirty if Perdikkas is otherwise occupied.”

“That’s not the freedom I was envisioning,” Mydei says. “Conditional release seems more like it...”

Peucesta allows himself the faintest hint of a smile. “For someone who just dominated a race, you complain a remarkable amount.”

“It keeps me grounded.”

“I wish you’d picked meditation.”

Mydei glances back toward the paddock—the flags still snapping in the heat, the hum of generators, the mechanics laughing over loose cables and empty cups.

He likes this part. The noise. The chaos. The clarity of being wanted for exactly one thing, and doing it well.

He straightens his clothes, wipes champagne from his cheek, and follows Peucesta onward.

The day isn’t done yet.

But for now, it feels—quietly, stubbornly—good to still be here.

Mydei rubs at his cheek one last time, finally dislodging the stubborn fleck of glitter that’s been haunting him since the podium. It sticks briefly to his thumb like it’s considering making a comeback, then he wipes it on the inside of his sleeve and calls it a day.

Around him, the team disperses in the familiar, post-race scramble. Someone’s arguing with a crate that refuses to roll straight. Someone else is power-walking while chugging coffee that smells aggressive enough to qualify as a biohazard. A pair of mechanics are laughing too loudly about something that definitely involved a near-miss and a lot of swearing.

Normal. Comfortingly so.

He falls into step beside Peucesta, who’s walking with the unhurried confidence of a man who knows exactly where he’s going and exactly how annoyed he’ll be when he gets there. His tablet is already out, thumb scrolling, expression caught somewhere between focused and quietly judgmental.

Without looking up, Peucesta says, “If anyone asks about your father today, blink twice and I’ll have them escorted into the sun.”

Mydei snorts. “Is that in the official media protocol?”

“It’s a footnote,” Peucesta replies. “Right under ‘smile politely’ and ‘do not commit international incidents.’”

“That feels like a high bar.”

“You clear it inconsistently. It comes with your background.”

The corner of Mydei’s mouth ticks up. Peucesta never tries to be funny, which somehow makes it worse—or better, depending on who you ask. Perdikkas once claimed it was a choice. Peucesta denied this with great offense and absolutely no conviction.

They pass Hephaestion, who’s leaned against a stack of tires and talking with Leonnius in low, animated tones.

“I’m just saying,” Leonnius insists, hands moving like he’s diagramming a crime scene, “that if he keeps doing that, I’m going to start aging in dog years.”

“You age in dog years already,” Hephaestion says mildly. “Might as well already be in your 80s.”

Leonnius points at Mydei as he passes. “You hear that? Zero support. None.”

“You’re still here,” Mydei says. “That means I did my job.”

“Barely,” Leonnius replies, but he’s grinning, eyes bright in that way that means he’s already replaying the race in his head, reliving every stupid, brilliant second.

The path toward the press pen opens up ahead, wider than the rest of the paddock, and the noise shifts again—voices rising, cameras clicking, the unmistakable hum of attention. It’s always louder there, which unfortunately never fails to give him a headache.

Peucesta slows half a step, scanning ahead.

“There’s a crowd forming,” he says. “Not the usual configuration.”

Mydei glances up. Beyond the media cluster, there’s a different knot of people—less frantic, more deliberate. Suits mixed with streetwear. Federation badges held just a little higher. A ripple of excitement that feels curated.

“Huh,” Mydei says. “Someone brought something with them.”

“Yes,” Peucesta agrees. “And unfortunately, it’s contagious.”

They walk a little farther. The squeals crest, then settle into a buzz of recognition.

Peucesta tilts his tablet, checks something, then sighs through his nose.

“Well,” he says. “That explains it.”

Mydei raises a brow. “You’re going to make me ask, aren’t you.”

“I am,” Peucesta says, deadpan. “Because if I volunteer this information, you’ll stop walking.”

“Now I’m definitely stopping.”

“Aglaea’s here.”

That does it.

Mydei actually slows, turning his head this time. “Aglaea as in—”

“As in that one,” Peucesta says. “And yes, she brought half her orbit with her.”

Mydei exhales, something between a laugh and a resigned sound of acceptance. “At a race weekend.”

“She doesn’t do coincidences,” Peucesta replies. “If she’s here, it’s because she wants to be seen being here.”

That tracks.

Aglaea has always been like that. The kind of woman who never raises her voice because she doesn’t need to. Mydei’s met her exactly twice before in an official setting, both times in rooms where everyone else was pretending not to be nervous.

He glances toward the cluster again, more curious than wary now.

“Should I say hello?” he asks.

Peucesta gives him a look. “You’re a race winner walking through her field of vision. If you don’t, she’ll remember.”

“Is that a threat?”

“It’s an observation.”

They angle slightly, skirting the edge of the gathering. Aglaea stands near the center, engaged in conversation with a Federation representative who looks like he’s concentrating very hard on not sweating through his suit. She’s dressed impeccably, but not stiffly—tailored and fashionable as always. There’s a mellow look to her expression that doesn’t quite reach her eyes, paired with the kind of polite humor that seems to land with surgical precision.

She laughs at something the rep says, brief and genuine, then corrects him immediately after. The rep nods like he’s been blessed.

Mydei huffs softly. “She hasn’t changed.”

“She has,” Peucesta says. “She just got better at hiding it.”

That’s when Peucesta’s gaze flicks sideways, sharp and assessing.

“…Huh.”

Mydei follows it automatically.

At first, nothing stands out. Just another figure on the fringe of the group, half a step back from Aglaea, posture loose, hands tucked casually into the pockets of a hoodie that looks wildly out of place among the suits.

He almost looks like he wandered in by accident.

Almost.

Mydei keeps walking, brain already categorizing and discarding. Some consultant, maybe. A friend. A relative. Someone waiting their turn.

Then the man shifts.

Just slightly. Weight rolling from one foot to the other. Head tilting as he listens.

The light catches his face.

A flash of white at the temple. Not dyed—natural, threaded through his messy hair. A familiar line along his cheekbone, a scar Mydei has seen before, though never like this. Not in person. Not close enough to count the years in it.

Mydei’s steps slow.

He doesn’t stop outright. That would draw attention. But something inside him does—a quiet, internal halt, like a handbrake pulled too hard.

The atmosphere feels different here. Cooler. Sharp with something clean and almost medicinal, a scent that tugs at a memory he can’t immediately place.

The man looks up.

Not at Mydei. Not yet.

But the angle of his face, the set of his shoulders, the way he occupies space without claiming it—

Mydei’s stomach drops.

Recognition doesn’t arrive as a thought. It arrives as a certainty.

He knows that silhouette.

His breath catches, shallow and involuntary, and for the first time all day, the noise of the paddock fades into something distant and indistinct.

Aglaea turns slightly, saying something to the man at her shoulder.

He responds quietly.

The sound of his voice reaches Mydei a second later—low, even, unhurried —and it lands like a physical thing.

Mydei stops.

Fully this time.

Whatever he was about to say to Aglaea evaporates. Whatever plan he had dissolves. All that’s left is the undeniable, impossible fact standing a few meters away, wearing a hoodie like this is just another afternoon.

Oh.

Oh.

His pulse spikes, loud in his ears, as the man turns—finally—into full view.

What the hell.

Aglaea finishes her conversation mid-sentence, expression sharpening as new information slots into place. She steps aside with practiced ease, clearing the narrow corridor through the paddock like she’s redirecting foot traffic without ever raising her voice.

He passes through the opening she creates.

Mydei’s brain supplies a dozen reasonable explanations in rapid succession. Assistant. Consultant. Someone late to something important. Someone who belongs here in a way that has nothing to do with—

Aglaea says his name, casual as breathing.

“—Phainon.”

He turns at the sound of it. She angles her phone toward him; he leans in just enough to glance at the screen, shoulder nearly brushing hers. Whatever she’s showing him earns a quiet hum of acknowledgment, something that sounds suspiciously like amusement.

He says a few words—too low to catch over the paddock noise—but Aglaea’s mouth curves, sharp and fond in equal measure. She taps the screen once, decisive, and pockets the phone.

“All right,” she says. “Go.”

Phainon nods. Easy. Comfortable. He shifts his weight and steps away from her—

—and starts walking straight toward Mydei.

Oh.

Mydei doesn’t move. He tells himself it’s because the walkway is crowded, because stepping aside now would be awkward, because he’s perfectly capable of behaving like a normal human being.

None of that helps his pulse, which decides this is an excellent moment to start misbehaving.

The hoodie is soft-looking, sleeves pushed up just enough to reveal strong forearms, and Mydei’s brain immediately files that away as deeply unhelpful information.

By the time Phainon reaches him, Mydei is acutely aware of everything: the lingering heat under his race suit, the faint thrum of generators, the way his heartbeat seems to have climbed into his throat and refuses to come down.

Phainon slows.

Not stopping at first—just easing his stride, attention sliding sideways as he registers Mydei’s presence. Their shoulders nearly brush as he passes, close enough that Mydei catches a clean, cool scent that cuts through the paddock haze.

Then Phainon stops.

It’s brief. Barely more than a beat.

His hand comes up, light and sure, settling on Mydei’s shoulder like it belongs there. The contact is warm through the fabric, deliberate without being strange. Familiar, somehow, even though they’ve never met like this.

Phainon looks at him then—really looks. His gaze lingers, curious and bright in a way that feels chosen.

“Congrats,” he says. His voice is calm, textured, pitched low enough that it feels like it’s meant just for Mydei. “That last lap was beautiful.”

The word lands clean and devastating.

Mydei’s breath stutters before he can stop it. His heart kicks, hard enough that he’s suddenly grateful for the noise around them, for the way the paddock swallows small, human reactions whole.

Beautiful.

He’s heard fast. Aggressive. Controlled. Stupidly brave. He’s heard worse. He’s heard better. But beautiful—

That’s different.

Phainon’s thumb shifts slightly where it rests, a subtle press, as if punctuating the compliment. His mouth curves—not quite a smile, but something close enough to promise one later.

Mydei opens his mouth. His brain offers him nothing useful. Gratitude tangles with surprise, admiration with something warmer and more—ahem.

Before he can commit to a sentence, someone calls Phainon’s name from further down the walkway.

Phainon glances over his shoulder, then back at Mydei. The hand on his shoulder lifts, fingers trailing just enough to register as intentional.

“Enjoy the rest of it,” he adds, easy. “You earned it.”

Then he’s gone—already moving, already folding back into the flow of the paddock like this was just another stop along the way.

Mydei stays where he is.

The apology floats overhead for the third time, airy and well-rehearsed, the kind that’s meant for everyone and no one at once.

“I’m terribly sorry for the inconvenience—”

Mydei moves with the practiced economy of someone who has learned how to exist in narrow spaces without apologizing for his shoulders. Business class smells faintly of lavender wipes, coffee that’s already gone cold, and the hum of recycled air that makes every flight feel like it’s happening inside a very expensive refrigerator. Someone ahead of him keeps turning with a backpack that swings wide enough to qualify as a public safety hazard, so Mydei angles his carry-on closer to his leg and sidesteps it skillfully.

Behind him, Hephaestion follows, posture rigid, expression locked into that familiar look of I should be anywhere else. Cipher brings up the rear, utterly unbothered by the universe’s obvious commitment to making this day interesting.

Mydei reaches his row, glances down at the number, then up—

—and stops.

Phainon is already there, settled into the window seat with the confidence of someone who boarded early and assumed the world would cooperate. One arm rests easily on the armrest, long legs angled just enough to avoid blocking the aisle. He looks up at the same moment Mydei looks at him.

They register each other in the same beat.

They quickly share the realization of logistical overlap.

The flight attendant hustles back down the aisle, breath a little fast, tablet hugged to her chest. “Yes—about that. We had a system error and accidentally assigned two passengers to fourteen A.”

Across the aisle, Hephaestion drops into fourteen C and immediately lowers his head. Cipher slides into fourteen D with suspicious grace, presses her lips together, and vibrates with suppressed laughter.

Mydei doesn’t hesitate. He barely even sighs.

“He can keep it,” he says, already shifting his bag.

Phainon blinks once. Polite. Almost startled, like he had expected at least a brief standoff over the window. “Oh. Thank you.”

It’s genuine, too, which somehow makes Mydei’s chest do something unhelpful.

He slips into the next seat after sorting it out with the flight attendant, and buckles in without fuss. Business class, at least, offers the dignity of armrests that exist and legroom that doesn’t feel punitive. He settles back, shoulders easing.

Small mercies.

Phainon glances over again, like he’s still recalibrating. “If you want the window later,” he adds, “I don’t mind switching.”

Mydei meets his gaze, the corner of his mouth lifting just enough to count as a smile. “I’m good. Aisle’s fine.”

Phainon studies him for a second longer than necessary, then nods, apparently satisfied. He turns back toward the window, though his knee remains angled just slightly toward Mydei, a detail that Mydei notices and absolutely does not overthink.

Hephaestion exhales through his nose. Cipher finally breaks, leaning forward just enough to murmur, “This is already better than in-flight entertainment.”

Mydei doesn’t look at her. He closes his eyes instead, lets his head rest back against the seat, and listens to the soft choreography of a plane preparing to leave the ground—bins clicking shut, seatbelts snapping, the murmur of strangers settling into shared air.

Beside him, Phainon shifts, the faint brush of fabric close enough to feel without touching.

It’s just a seat mix-up.

Just a flight.

And somehow, already, it feels like the universe is smirking.

An hour into the flight, the cabin settles into its second personality.

The initial bustle has thinned into a low, collective murmur. Overhead lights glow dimmer now, softened to something gentler on the eyes. A flight attendant nudges a cart down the aisle with careful precision, glassware chiming softly as she pauses to pour water, then wine, then coffee that smells stronger than it has any right to at this altitude. Across the aisle, a man in a pressed jacket leans toward his seatmate and whispers with the intensity of someone discussing a hostile takeover. Two rows back, a child hums to herself, tuneless and content, her socked feet tapping the seat in front of her in a rhythm only she understands.

The plane hums steadily beneath it all, a constant presence rather than a disturbance.

Phainon sits with the window shade half-lowered, sunlight catching along the edge of his hair and the sharp line of his cheek. One hand rests in his lap, fingers loosely intertwined, the other braced against the armrest. He looks out at the clouds with quiet attention, almost absentmindedly.

Mydei sits beside him, posture relaxed in theory, attentive in practice. He reads the same paragraph on his screen for the third time and absorbs none of it. His awareness keeps orbiting sideways, drawn by small details he pretends not to catalogue. The steady rhythm of Phainon’s breathing. The way his foot shifts when the plane makes a gentle adjustment. The faint scent of soap and something honey-adjacent.

Around them, their entourage does a poor job pretending they are uninvolved.

Hephaestion adjusts his headphones, glancing over the top of them like a long-suffering chaperone. Cipher watches openly, tablet forgotten, chin propped in her palm. Castorice cranes just enough to confirm her suspicions, then settles back with an expression of vindicated patience. Even Aglaea, further back, meets Mydei’s eyes for half a second and lifts her brows with serene expectation.

The universe continues its refusal to offer a convenient opening.

But then the plane gives a small, passing jolt.

It rolls through the cabin with the mild indifference of weather doing what it does. Drinks ripple in their cups. The overhead bins murmur. A few passengers shift, then settle again.

Mydei’s body reacts faster than his mind.

His shoulders draw in. His hand tightens around the armrest. His breath stutters before smoothing out again, measured and controlled.

Phainon turns his head.

The movement stays small, respectful of shared space, but his attention sharpens immediately. His gaze flicks to Mydei’s hand, then to his face, clocking his reading posture and tension.

“Does turbulence bother you?” he asks, voice low enough that it stays between them, calm without softness that might sound patronizing.

Mydei exhales, slightly relieved as the opportunity to talk revealed itself. “It catches me off guard sometimes. I spend most of my time with the ground doing exactly what I expect it to.”

Phainon’s mouth curves, just barely. The expression carries recognition. “That makes sense. Things feels different when it comes from an engine you can feel responding.”

Mydei turns his head fully this time. “You too then? Turbulence, I mean.”

“I do,” Phainon replies. He shifts in his seat, angling himself a little more toward Mydei without fully abandoning the window. “I had the same adjustment period when my schedule started involving longer flights. The lack of feedback takes getting used to.”

Mydei feels the tightness in his shoulders ease. “That’s a good way to put it. Feedback. I trust turbulence more when I know what caused it.”

Phainon nods, thoughtful. “Patterns help. I tend to map them even when it’s unnecessary. Besides, the pilots usually know what they’re doing.”

“Usually… that sounds reassuring,” Mydei says, a smile pulling at his mouth.

Phainon’s gaze lingers on that smile longer than required. He doesn’t look away quickly.

“My schedule lets me fly more often than I’d like,” Phainon continues. “You develop habits. Certain playlists. Certain books. Something repetitive enough to distract you.”

“What works for you?” Mydei asks, curious.

Phainon considers the question as if it deserves proper treatment. “Manual hobbies. Things that occupy the hands without demanding the mind. I picked up crocheting a few years ago.”

Mydei blinks. “Seriously?” He almost winced at his tone. He hadn’t meant it in a strange way. Just—well—he didn’t seem the type.

“Entirely,” Phainon says. “Scarves at first. Then blankets. My friends benefit greatly from my inability to stand still.”

Mydei’s interest sharpens, immediate and unfiltered. “That’s actually impressive. I tried knitting once and managed to turn yarn into something… interesting to say the least. My parents weren’t pleased.”

Phainon’s lips part, a soft sound leaving him that sits somewhere between a laugh and a fond hum. “That stage passes. Muscle memory settles in, and it becomes meditative.”

“I can see that,” Mydei says. “There’s something comforting about repetitive motion. I do that with mechanical work sometimes. Taking things apart, putting them back together even when they don’t need it.”

Phainon’s attention fixes on him fully now. “You do your own adjustments?”

“When I can,” Mydei answers. “It helps me understand where limits actually live. Plus Peuc—sorry, my manager appreciates when I keep myself busy in productive ways.”

Phainon studies him, eyes tracing Mydei’s expression as though committing it to memory. “That aligns with how you race.”

Mydei’s pauses. “You’ve watched me more than once?”

“I have,” Phainon says. He shifts his arm on the armrest, close enough that the heat from his sleeve brushes Mydei’s forearm. “Your decision-making tightened midway through the season. The exits became more confident. You trusted the car and yourself earlier.”

The cabin fades a little around them. Mydei’s pulse makes itself known.

“That adjustment came after a shoulder issue,” Mydei says. “I had to rework how I compensated. Hearing someone noticed such a small detail feels… surprising.”

Phainon continued further, giving Mydei a languid smile. “Details like that stand out when someone interests me.”

He says it plainly without flourish. His gaze meets Mydei’s and stays there, unabashed.

Mydei absorbs the words slowly. “I spent time studying your footage too,” he admits, the honesty slipping out with a sincerity that surprises him. “Your consistency taught me a lot.”

Phainon’s expression changes to be slightly more softer. “I’m glad it reached you.”

Cipher finally looks away, satisfied. Hephaestion exhales and settles deeper into his seat. Somewhere behind them, a flight attendant laughs quietly with a passenger.

Phainon turns back toward the window, though his knee stays angled toward Mydei, presence still attentive. “If the flight grows restless later,” he says casually, “I can show you a stitch pattern. It passes time surprisingly well.”

Mydei perks up slightly. “I’d like that.”

And then because he can’t keep his mouth shut—

“Your footwork in Shanghai was clean, too.”

The words escape Mydei before he has time to filter them through dignity, discretion, or any of the internal safeguards that usually prevent him from confessing years of accumulated admiration in public seating arrangements.

Phainon turns toward him fully this time. His eyebrows lift, just slightly, a small break in his carefully even composure.

“Shanghai,” he repeats, rolling the word once like he’s checking its weight. “That was… a while ago.”

“Yeah,” Mydei says, nodding with an ease he does not feel. His hand makes a small, unconscious gesture in the air, fingers tracing an invisible arc before he realizes he’s doing it and pulls it back to the armrest. “Still good.”

A beat passes.

The program had aired briefly, shuffled into an awkward time slot, then vanished into archive purgatory after production issues. People who remembered it tended to remember the controversy, the cancellation, the disappointment. Very few remembered the skating itself.

Phainon’s expression shifts. Surprise flickers there, followed by something else. His expression was unreadable now as his gaze lingered.

They both turn away at the same time—two men who absolutely do not know how to deal with sincerity.

Mydei decided to focus on somewhere behind them,  where someone laughs softly at something on their phone. A welcomed distraction.

Phainon shifts in his seat, a subtle roll of his ankle like he’s checking the joint out of habit. The motion stays small, but Mydei clocks it instantly, the detail slipping neatly into that mental drawer he keeps labeled things to revisit later when he has time to worry properly.

He closes the drawer.

Their elbows brush against the shared armrest.

The contact carries weight disproportionate to its size.

Mydei clears his throat, mostly to force himself forward before his brain builds an obstacle course out of hesitation.

“You know,” he starts, voice settling into something steadier, “that performance you did that season… I really enjoyed it.”

Phainon turns toward him again, this time without surprise. Curiosity sits openly on his face, patient and attentive in a way that makes words line up more easily for Mydei.

“It was elegant,” Mydei continues, leaning slightly forward now, hands moving again despite himself. “Your transitions stayed fluid even when the tempo shifted. Most skaters tighten there, but you let the phrasing continue. The way you carried momentum through the diagonals made the whole thing feel intentional, and it matched the music in guiding it.”

He stops gesturing when he realizes how animated he’s become, fingers curling against his palm. A quiet laugh slips out of him, soft and disbelieving. “Sorry. I—this stuff sticks with me.”

Phainon listens without interruption.

“I appreciated the restraint,” Mydei adds, slower now, choosing his words carefully. “There was direction in it I admired. Everything had purpose.”

His heart rate picks up, recognizing familiar emotional territory.

“And honestly—before that too. Everything you did stood out. You had this way of committing fully without overplaying it. I used to—”

He stops.

Abruptly.

Because the next sentence waiting in the wings is I used to watch you for hours when I was figuring out if my dream was worth fighting my whole life for, and that feels like a confession best saved for a universe with fewer seatbelts.

He reroutes with practiced grace.

“Anyway,” he says, smoothing his tone, professionalism sliding neatly back into place, “I wanted to ask how you’ve been doing since—well….”

The question hangs there, gentle and unfinished.

The seatbelt sign chimes overhead.

Almost immediately, the plane hits a pocket of turbulence.

A toddler across the aisle squeals with delight, feet kicking happily as the cabin jostles. A flight attendant appears with impeccable timing, reminding everyone to remain seated, voice calm and reassuring.

The moment disperses just like that.

Mydei exhales, settling back into his seat, letting the interruption carry the intensity somewhere safer.

Phainon keeps his gaze on the window for a moment longer, watching coastline lights scatter beneath them like spilled constellations. When he speaks, his voice arrives softer, reflective.

“I like window seats,” he murmurs.

The shift feels natural, eased by the interruption rather than forced by it.

“They help me stay oriented,” he continues, fingers resting lightly against the armrest. “I sketch sometimes. Cities from above. Patterns in how places grow. It makes travel feel… tangible.”

Then he turns, offering Mydei a small, genuine smile.

“Thanks for letting me take this one.”

Mydei’s heart attempts to replicate the turbulence internally. Externally, he manages a composed nod.

“Of course.”

The rest of the flight stretches gently after that. Conversation resurfaces in quieter forms—shared stories about unexpected hobbies, Mydei admitting to his interest in Instruments and performing, Phainon listening with interest that lingers longer than required. Words come and go, punctuated by comfortable pauses that surprisingly don’t feel awkward.

By the time the wheels touch down, they’ve had three real conversations, fourteen accidental glances, and an impressive number of half-formed thoughts left suspended between them.

Cabin lights brighten. Passengers rise in slow, impatient clusters.

Phainon reaches for his bag first, pausing before stepping into the aisle. The pause feels deliberate.

He turns toward Mydei.

“Hey,” he says. “Thanks for the company.”

Mydei huffs a soft laugh. “We barely talked.”

Phainon’s smile deepens, like sunrise edging over a horizon.

“Still counts.”

Then, quietly—

“See you, Mydeimos.”

He merges into the flow of passengers, disappearing inch by inch as the crowd carries him away.

Mydei remains seated for a moment longer, pulse still racing like it has somewhere urgent to be. He stands once his expression settles, joining the slow procession toward the exit.

He tells himself the flight was uneventful.

His heartbeat suggests otherwise.

Chapter Summary

Four days of content farming, scenic “competitions,” and Cipher refusing to be stopped.

By Day Five, Mydei is watching figure skating practice in a cold rink, Phainon is being effortlessly charming on and off the ice, and both of them are losing a battle they didn’t realize they were fighting.

Chapter Notes

HAPPY LATE NEW YEAR!!! The pacing is a bit iffy in this but I hope y’all enjoy reading <333

The Salzburg International Sports Complex presented itself like a statement piece rather than a venue.

Everything gleamed with intention. Glass facades caught the Alps at precise angles, snow-bright peaks reflected so cleanly they looked painted. Walkways curved in gentle, deliberate lines, guiding foot traffic the way a conductor guides an orchestra. Even the cold carried structure—clean, alpine air that filled the lungs and snapped the senses awake.

It suited the crowd perfectly.

High-performance environments always attracted a certain species of person: sports scientists with color-coded lanyards, biomechanics specialists arguing about tendon elasticity over breakfast, federation officials in tailored coats discussing marginal gains like sacred scripture. Everywhere Mydei turned, someone wore a badge declaring a job title that sounded invented yet paid extremely well.

This week, Austria hosted two events simultaneously: the International High-Performance Athletic Symposium and a winter sports heritage showcase. Salzburg, ever proud of its ability to blend history with prestige, treated the overlap like a feature rather than a scheduling accident.

And because Austria adored symbolic invitations, Kremnos Apex received one.

Greek roots. Global reach. A racing dynasty polished enough for museum glass. And one infuriatingly photogenic heir who insisted his emotional attachment lay with tire degradation curves and braking points rather than the fact that half the attendees could trace their sponsorship pipeline back to his surname.

That heir walked the concourse right now, hands tucked into his coat, expression calm in a way that made publicists nervous.

Mydei.

Red Bull’s influence threaded through the symposium like an invisible watermark, turning the entire week into a bundled experience: paddock tours, cross-discipline panels, athlete showcases, and carefully “spontaneous” introductions. The atmosphere felt less like a conference and more like a grand experiment where someone mixed every competitive industry together and waited to see who bonded over protein shakes.

The morning passed smoothly enough.

Luggage reached them intact. Breakfast involved nodding politely through small talk while Leonnius explained, with evangelical passion, why Austrian pastries deserved a dedicated training exemption. Then came the biomechanics lecture Leonnius promised would change Mydei’s life and instead delivered a sobering reminder that letting Leonnius choose compulsory sessions ranked among his more questionable decisions.

Mydei endured it with the patience of an older sibling listening to a younger one explain something discovered five minutes ago.

After lunch, staff directed them toward the media pavilion for what the schedule described as a casual introduction.

Casual arrived carrying optimism.

They stepped outside, boots crunching softly against treated stone, Salzburg stretching wide and immaculate around them. Church spires punctured the skyline. Bells chimed somewhere distant. For a few seconds, the world felt composed.

Then sound arrived first.

A layered roar rolled around the corner—voices overlapping, camera shutters rattling, someone calling out in sharp Austrian German with the practiced urgency of local press. A cluster of fans surged forward, winter coats puffed like armor, phones already raised.

“Mydei—Herr Mydei—ein Moment!”

“Der junge Formel-1-Star—hier!”

The crowd thickened instantly, momentum building like snow sliding off a roof.

Leonnius froze for exactly half a second before instincts kicked in.

“MOVE—move, move, MOVE—!” he shouted, voice slicing through the noise as he threw his arms wide, attempting crowd control through sheer conviction.

Microphones appeared. A camera shoved close enough for Mydei to count eyelashes.

“Herr Mydei! Championship thoughts? Team rumors?”

Another voice snapped into English, bright and breathless. “Austria wants you for the cultural promo tonight—is that confirmed?”

Flash. Flash. Flash.

Leonnius planted his feet directly in the chaos, jacket flaring as he spun like a windmill with a press badge.

“BACK—back, BACK—!” he roared, vowels stretching with effort. “He is off-schedule! This introduction happens later! You are improvising and I refuse to participate—MYDEI! STOP MOVING LIKE YOU’RE MADE OF SOAP AND HELP—!”

Mydei sighed softly.

Years of threading a car through shrinking gaps at impossible speeds translated beautifully to this moment. He pivoted, slipped between two camera operators arguing about framing, hooked a steady arm around Leonnius’s elbow, and guided them sideways through a narrow opening like a practiced dance.

“I mentioned the private route,” Mydei said calmly as they moved.

“That route required staff clearance we lacked,” Leonnius puffed, boots skidding slightly as he kept up. “Also, I expected restraint. Alpine serenity. Neutral energy.”

“Austrians stay calm,” Mydei replied. “Until sports enter the equation.”

“That looked calm to you?!”

“You would enjoy Italian press,” Mydei added, voice thoughtful. “They treat publicists like communal property.”

“For what purpose?”

“Negotiation.”

They reached the frosted glass wall marking federation-only access. Security stood posted there, jackets crisp, expressions carved from stone. A single look sent the crowd stalling like traffic meeting a closed tunnel.

Inside, warmth replaced the bite of winter. The hallway hummed with low conversation and distant footsteps, insulated from the frenzy outside.

Leonnius leaned against the wall, hands braced on his knees, breath coming in exaggerated pulls.

“This,” he said between inhales, “qualifies as hostile terrain.”

Mydei waited beside him, unruffled, watching color return to his friend’s face.

“When we get home,” Leonnius continued, straightening with renewed dignity, “I will draft a letter. Ten pages. Structured. Passionate.”

“You will reach page two,” Mydei said gently, as if talking to an injured animal.

Leonnius paused. Considered. “A pastry will intervene.”

“Always does.”

They shared a grin and started down the hallway at an easier pace, footsteps echoing softly.

Leonnius lets the silence breathe for exactly three steps.

Then—casually, cruelly—he glances sideways.

“Oh,” he says, tone light. “Speaking of distractions. You know Aglaea’s skating crew? The one you’re very normal about?”

Mydei doesn’t even turn his head. “I am extremely normal about everyone.”

“That pause you just took,” Leonnius continues, unfazed, “was not convincing.”

“I paused because I’m walking,” Mydei says. “People do that.”

“Sure,” Leonnius hums. “Anyway. Cipher went live.”

That earns him a look.

Leonnius smiles with the quiet satisfaction of an older brother who has located the exact pressure point and applied it gently, lovingly, with intent.

“She does that thing,” he adds, already unlocking his phone, “where she pretends it’s spontaneous but somehow the lighting is perfect and her mic is crystal clear. Very organic. Very her.”

“I don’t care,” Mydei says immediately.

“You shouldn’t,” Leonnius agrees. “Except Phainon is with them, and statistically speaking, Cipher has never missed an opportunity to aim a camera at something interesting.”

Mydei stops walking.

Just for a beat.

Leonnius does not comment on this. He simply taps the screen and tilts the phone.

The livestream opens mid-motion.

⸻

● LIVE—@cipherontherun

3.8k viewers 💬 chat scrolling fast...

Cipher’s face fills the screen, framed by soft daylight and her own impeccable confidence. She walks backward down a wide corridor, camera steady, voice playful.

“Okay, okay—hi, hello, good morning to everyone who skipped work for this, I see you,” she says, flashing a grin. “We’re backstage at the Salzburg complex, which means yes, it’s cold, yes, it’s fancy, and yes, everyone here looks like they drink something green before sunrise.”

The comments scroll fast.

Ciphersthickthighs: omg is this the symposium trashcanenthusiast: show us the athletes 👀 trailblaze_deeznuts: cipher the eyeliner??? pompomfanclub: is castorice there???

Cipher pivots the camera with a practiced flick of her wrist.

Castorice appears in frame, bundled neatly in a cream coat, clipboard tucked to her chest. She blinks, then smiles and gives a small wave.

“Oh—hi,” she says softly. “Good morning. We’re in the warm-up corridor. The airflow here is actually designed to reduce muscle stiffness before—”

Cipher leans into frame, “She’s being humble. She could talk about this for an hour and I’d monetize every minute.”

Castorice laughs, cheeks pink, and continues anyway, voice gentle and focused. “It helps with temperature regulation between sessions. Especially for ankles and knees.”

The chat explodes.

silverwolf_alt_acc_7: CASTORICE MY BELOVED kafka_step_on_me: ankles?? march7thbias: is PHD there???

Mydei’s attention sharpens so fast it surprises even him.

The camera swings again, catching movement at the edge of the frame— white jacket, familiar posture, the suggestion of a profile—

Cipher reacts instantly.

“Oh! Nope,” she sings, turning the phone toward the floor with theatrical grace. “Some people are off-limits today, folks. Mystery is good for engagement.”

cloudknightirl: NOOOO this_is_not_mara: cipher we saw that

imbibitor_lmfao: was that PHD?? FoxgirlUnionRep: rewind!!!

Cipher grins at the screen, unfazed. “Respecting boundaries builds trust. Trust builds loyalty. Loyalty builds—well, you know.”

She winks and lifts the camera again, this time catching her boots, the polished floor, the hum of voices around them.

“Anyway, we’re heading to warm-ups. Stick around. Or don’t. I’ll be here regardless.”

⸻

The stream cuts as Leonnius lowers the phone.

He glances up.

Mydei is staring at nothing in particular with the intensity of someone replaying a single blurred frame in high definition inside his skull.

“They seem fine,” Leonnius says mildly. “Busy. Productive. Living their lives.”

Mydei swallows. “Good.”

His voice behaves. His face behaves. His internal world is doing something else entirely.

He adjusts his jacket, then does it again, because his hands need somewhere to go.

“That was,” he says, carefully neutral, “informative.”

Leonnius snorts. “You leaned forward.”

“I did not.”

“You absolutely did.”

They resume walking, footsteps echoing toward the elevator bank. Around them, delegates drift past in clusters, laughter bouncing off glass walls, the low murmur of multilingual conversations threading through the space. Someone nearby argues cheerfully about funding allocations. Another group poses for photos beside a banner.

Life keeps moving.

Mydei keeps pace, eyes forward.

“Well,” he adds, tone easy, a thin smile threatening to give him away, “it’s not as if we’re meeting anytime soon.”

The elevator doors slide open with a soft chime.

Leonnius steps inside first, glancing back with a look that carries years of shared history, shared secrets, and the unshakable certainty that this will be unbearable interesting.

“Mhm,” he says. “Let’s see how long that lasts.”

Well.

That was optimistic of him.

Mydei had said—confidently, even—it’s not as if we’re meeting anytime soon.

Austria, apparently, took that as a personal challenge.

The festival hadn’t officially started, which meant Salzburg existed in its liminal state: too early for crowds, too late for privacy. Athletes, teams, sponsors, and organizers drifted through the city like migratory birds who all booked the same cafés. Lanyards tucked into jackets. Sunglasses worn indoors. That specific buzz of people pretending they weren’t already on.

Mydei’s hotel sat just off the old town, stone walls and pleasantly quiet hallways. From his window, he could see the edge of the Hohensalzburg

Fortress if he leaned far enough, the silhouette cutting clean against the morning sky.

Everything was scheduled. Predictable, even.

Which made it deeply irritating that he had already spotted Phainon three separate times in under twenty-four hours.

Not close encounters. Flashes. White hair across a lobby. A familiar stride disappearing through glass doors. A gentle laugh—unmistakable, kind— echoing somewhere behind him while he pretended very hard not to turn around.

Hephaestion noticed by the second sighting.

By the third, he’d stopped pretending not to.

“This is getting statistically interesting,” Hephaestion said mildly over breakfast, eyes following Mydei’s gaze as it tracked, again, to absolutely nothing. “You want to tell me something?”

Mydei buttered his toast with unnecessary focus. “Austria is small.”

“Salzburg is not that small.”

“Relative to the universe,” Mydei said, and stood up before the conversation could continue.

The collision happened an hour later.

He’d ducked out early, intent on walking through the contemporary wing of the Mozarteum before it filled with people who liked to stand too close while pretending not to read plaques. The hallway was long, sculptures arranged meticulously under soft, indirect lighting.

He rounded a corner.

And walked directly into a chest.

Unfortunately, not a shoulder. Nor an arm.

A chest.

Solid, warm, and—unhelpfully—at the exact height where Mydei’s forward momentum carried him straight in. His hands came up on reflex, palms spreading to brace—

—and found give.

He didn’t register it immediately.

What he registered was the warmth. The faint smell of clean fabric and some type of perfume. The way the impact knocked the air out of him just enough that his body decided leaning was easier than correcting.

For half a second—maybe longer—his cheek pressed in.

It was… comfortable.

Soft in a way that didn’t match the rest of the frame beneath it. Solid underneath, sure, but cushioned. The kind of deceptive softness that absorbed pressure instead of rejecting it.

Mydei exhaled.

Almost sighed.

His eyes drifted shut on instinct, brain lagging behind sensation like a system booting up.

Somewhere above him, someone made a startled sound—short, sharp, surprised—but didn’t step back.

Didn’t move at all, actually.

Which was odd.

Mydei adjusted his grip slightly, fingers curling without thinking, as if to steady himself better. His thumbs pressed in—

Oh.

Oh no.

Awareness snapped into place like a safety harness engaging too late.

He stiffened, heat flooding his face as his brain finally caught up to the fact that he was not, in fact, leaning against a wall or a conveniently placed cushion.

He was holding a man’s chest.

With both hands.

And his cheek was still there.

He jerked back like he’d been burned, hands dropping instantly as he took a step away, throat clearing hard enough to feel it.

“I—sorry. I wasn’t—” Mydei stopped himself, because continuing would only make it worse.

Phainon stood where he’d been, looking down at him with a surprised expression. His posture stayed loose, unbothered, like nothing unusual had happened at all.

White hair, slightly mussed. Broad shoulders under a fitted jacket. That familiar, unfairly handsome face.

His eyes flicked briefly to Mydei’s hands, then back up.

“…You okay?” Phainon asked.

His voice was low, still rough around the edges like he’d only been awake long enough to exist, not enough to filter himself.

Mydei nodded once. Then again, because the first one felt insufficient. “Yeah. Fine. Sorry about that.”

Phainon hummed, considering. “You caught yourself fast.”

Mydei blinked. “I… what?”

“You shifted your weight before you fell,” Phainon said, entirely serious. “Good reflexes.”

A beat.

“That was not—” Mydei stopped. Tried again. “That was an accident.”

“I know.”

Phainon smiled.

It was easy. Uncomplicated. Like the idea of Mydei slamming into him had not lodged anywhere embarrassing in his mind at all.

“It’s my fault too,” he added. “I wasn’t watching where I was going.”
